title: Evaluating Generate–Validate–Repair Pipelines for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study comparing a baseline single‑shot LLM configuration generator against a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline (with a canary stage) on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus (2000 paired episodes). The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses) and validation used a deterministic digital‑twin validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one sampled initial generation per task was deterministically reused by both arms; downstream validation and the permitted single repair call (guarded arm only) were the only mechanisms for paired outcome differences. Observed outcomes: baseline safe‑deploy = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded safe‑deploy = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference = 0.005 (n11=995, n10=5, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered primary inferential test (exact two‑sided McNemar) yields p = 0.0625 (not < 0.05). The preregistered secondary descriptive summary (paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729) is [0.001, 0.01]. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred and total model calls used = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5). We report the exact McNemar result as the preregistered confirmatory outcome, present the bootstrap CI as a secondary descriptive summary, explicitly label a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) as exploratory/post‑hoc (it was not specified in the frozen preregistration), and interpret the small absolute guarded benefit in light of sparse discordant counts, high baseline validity, validator scope, and the shared_initial_candidate design.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation for network operations promises reduced manual effort but raises safety risks: multi‑step sequencing errors, transient invariants violations, and protected‑field interference can convert plausible command sequences into harmful actions. Prior surveys and controlled studies document LLM hallucination, high prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures that affect code and configuration generation; such evidence motivates architectures that pair generative models with deterministic validators and bounded repair procedures. This work asks a narrowly scoped, preregistered question suitable for a paired design: when baseline and guarded conditions begin from the exact same sampled initial candidate (shared_initial_candidate semantics), to what degree can a downstream deterministic validator plus a single allowed repair call (guarded pipeline with canary) improve paired safe‑deploy outcomes compared with reusing the same initial candidate unmodified (baseline)?

We contribute: (1) a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment (cand‑003‑stud‑001) that isolates purely downstream validator/repair effects under shared_initial_candidate semantics; (2) a complete execution and analysis run (1000 complete pairs, deterministic reconciliation, and archived validator traces) with full accounting of model calls and repair stage counts; and (3) an evidence‑grounded interpretation that reconciles the preregistered power assumptions with the observed high baseline validity and sparse repairs, clarifying what this specific estimand measures and does not measure. All preregistration, execution manifests, raw outputs, and analysis artifacts are archived with the run and summarized below.
sections.related_work:
Empirical surveys and controlled experiments demonstrate that LLM outputs for structured tasks (code, configurations, plans) are susceptible to hallucination and prompt sensitivity that materially affect correctness [1],[2]. Methods that constrain decoding or apply schema‑aware generation reduce syntactic and executability errors in structured domains, though much of the strongest evidence originates outside NetOps and transfer depends on validator and tool fidelity [3],[4]. Recent NetOps and agentic‑AI system papers emphasize verifier‑assisted repair, guarded architectures, and governance/proof‑carrying proposals that aim to mitigate automation risks; these works report prototype improvements but stress dependence on validator coverage, protocol enforcement, and auditability rather than on any single model's inherent reliability [5],[6],[7].

Our study complements these works by preregistering a paired comparison whose estimand measures the incremental effect of deterministic downstream validation and a limited repair budget when the initial candidate is held constant across conditions. This design avoids conflating downstream interventions with first‑pass prompt/decoding differences and thereby clarifies what downstream verifier/repair layers can and cannot achieve under tightly controlled conditions.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen design: The study preregistration (cand‑003‑stud‑001) was finalized and frozen before any hosted‑model invocation. Key preregistered elements: confirmatory paired binary design; task_count = 1000 deterministic tasks from the challenging_workflow_stress_v1 synthetic corpus; generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (exactly one sampled initial generation per pair deterministically reused by both conditions); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; planned_hosted_model_calls = 2000 (the adapter semantics allow the guarded arm to use its single permitted repair call but the executor ultimately bounds model calls to the recorded totals). The preregistered primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the preregistered primary inferential test is the exact two‑sided McNemar test applied to the 2×2 contingency table formed by paired outcomes. Secondary preregistered summaries included a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) and sensitivity analyses treating failed calls as unsafe. Multiplicity handling for secondary hypothesis claims was specified via Holm–Bonferroni.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and interpretive consequences: Under the archived generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate, both baseline and guarded episodes begin from the same sampled initial candidate; the guarded pipeline differs only by (a) deterministic validation that can reject/accept the candidate and (b) at most one permitted repair call that may produce a new candidate for re‑validation. Thus paired outcome differences can arise only from deterministic validator decisions and permitted repair(s); the design does not and cannot measure effects that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or constrained prompting arms that were not executed.

Model and runtime configuration: Declared model = gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses). The archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. The adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the validator/digital twin was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator version 5.0), which enforces workflow policies, required command presence and order, and protected‑field noninterference. Scoring was deterministic: scoring_rule = full_intent_constraint_validation, and scoring produced a binary safe‑deploy indicator where validity required satisfying all intent constraints encoded in the task manifest.

Task corpus and synthetic semantics: Tasks were drawn deterministically from the preregistered challenging_workflow_stress_v1 profile using the registered ordinal rule (task_count = 1000 unique task_indices). Task payloads include explicit required_sequence constraints, allowed_touched_fields, and an initial and expected_final_state; difficulty labels (very_hard, extreme) and dependency patterns were embedded in the task manifest and archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl. The validator evaluates candidate command sequences against those manifest constraints in a deterministic digital‑twin emulator.

Execution accounting and retries: The preregistered execution contract allowed retries only per the adapter's maximum_attempts_per_call = 1 and defined missingness treatments. The execution manifest (deterministic_reconciliation.json and execution manifest) records completed_episode_count = 2000, failed_episode_count = 0, hosted_model_call_event_count = 1005, stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation = 1000, repair = 5}, and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false. All seeds, selection rules, and analysis procedures were fixed pre‑execution.

Statistical analysis: The preregistered confirmatory test is exact two‑sided McNemar for the paired difference estimand (conditioning on total discordant count). The paired bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) was preregistered as a descriptive secondary summary. The preregistration's power_and_precision_plan specified a target effect of 0.15 with assumed baseline ≈0.60 (two‑sided α = 0.05) to achieve >80% power; these assumptions are recorded in the preregistration and are explicitly reconciled with the observed data in Results/Discussion below. Important preregistered caveat: the analysis executor implements exact McNemar (discrete small‑sample combinatorics) as the primary confirmatory procedure because it conditions on the scarce discordant outcomes and is robust to sparse discordance; bootstrapped intervals are reported only descriptively and can be sensitive to very small discordant counts.
sections.results:
Execution summary and accounting (artifact‑grounded): start 2026‑09‑01T06:31:07Z; completion 2026‑09‑01T08:38:57Z. Planned episodes = 2000; completed = 2000; failed = 0; complete_pairs = 1000. Provider‑call audit (deterministic_reconciliation.json): hosted_model_call_event_count = 1005; completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 1005; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0; cache_miss_count = 1005; stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 1000; repair = 5. Cross‑condition cache key reuse was not observed.

Paired outcomes and primary inferential result (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): contingency counts: n11 = 995 (both succeeded), n10 = 5 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded, guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). Observed success rates: baseline = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. The preregistered primary confirmatory test (exact two‑sided McNemar) yields p = 0.0625, which does not cross the preregistered two‑sided α = 0.05 threshold; thus the preregistered H1 is not supported by the confirmatory test.

Secondary descriptive summaries and sensitivity: The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) yields [0.001, 0.01] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). The bootstrap interval excludes zero owing to resampling variability dominated by the few discordant pairs; as discussed below, this descriptive summary is sensitive to very small discordant counts and must be interpreted in the context of the exact conditional McNemar test being the preregistered primary analysis. The one‑sided directional McNemar (guarded > baseline) returns p = 0.03125: this test was not enumerated in the frozen preregistration and therefore is reported here explicitly as exploratory/post‑hoc; it does not alter the preregistered confirmatory conclusion.

Repair invocation and mechanistic trace examples: Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred (repair stage_count = 5). Representative validator traces archived in execution/scoring artifacts show the validator applying required_sequence checks and protected_interface constraints to reject or accept the shared initial candidate; in each of the five repaired episodes the repair produced a corrected command ordering that restored compliance with the manifest's required_sequence and the validator then accepted the repaired candidate. Total model calls used = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5). All raw responses, provider call traces, validator traces, and the paired contingency CSV are archived with the run.
sections.discussion:
Inferential reconciliation: The preregistered primary inference is the exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625) and therefore the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis H1 is not supported at two‑sided α = 0.05. The paired bootstrap CI ([0.001, 0.01]) is a preregistered descriptive summary; its exclusion of zero arises from bootstrap sensitivity with extremely sparse discordant counts (n10=5, n01=0). Exact conditional tests (McNemar) properly account for the discrete combinatorics of the paired 2×2 table and were chosen a priori for this reason; readers should treat the bootstrap CI as contextual but not as overturning the preregistered confirmatory outcome.

Power and preregistration mismatch: The preregistered power plan assumed baseline ≈0.60 and a target absolute increase of 0.15 to attain >80% power under the planned task_count = 1000. The observed baseline success rate of 0.995 is far higher than that assumption, and the observed effect (0.005) is much smaller than the preregistered target. This mismatch materially reduces the design's sensitivity to detect small absolute gains: with baseline near unity almost no discordant pairs are expected, so even correct downstream interventions yield small discordant counts that make two‑sided exact tests insensitive at conventional α thresholds. We report this mismatch explicitly to caution against overinterpreting the small absolute guarded gain in contexts with already very high baseline validity.

Mechanistic implications: Under shared_initial_candidate semantics only downstream validator/repair actions can produce paired differences. The five successful repairs show that deterministic validator chains can correct particular ordering/sequence violations when the validator's coverage includes the violated rules. However, the low repair invocation count indicates either (a) the synthetic corpus produced few initial candidates that violated validator constraints, (b) the generator tended to produce valid candidates for this model+prompt setting, or (c) the validator's modeled constraint set did not capture other classes of semantic/policy errors. Distinguishing among these mechanistic possibilities requires broader experiments (varying repair budgets, validator coverage, and independent generation arms) that are outside this preregistered estimand.

Construct and external validity: The safe‑deploy binary outcome depends on the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 rule set (digital twin). That validator approximates operational policies but remains an abstraction of real, heterogeneous vendor networks and emergent multi‑device semantics. Consequently measured baseline success rates can be inflated if validator coverage omits critical policy checks; we therefore caution against generalizing these numeric success rates to production without broader validator diversity. Similarly, the single‑model scope (gpt‑5‑mini) prevents generalization across model families.

Operational implications and recommended follow‑ups: Artifact‑grounded evidence here shows that verifier‑guided safeguards can avert some unsafe outcomes in workflow settings, but measurable marginal gains depend strongly on baseline failure prevalence, validator sensitivity/coverage, and permitted repair budget. Follow‑ups should (1) evaluate independent first‑pass generation arms to measure prompt/decoding intervention effects; (2) vary the repair budget to quantify marginal repair utility; (3) expand validator suites and topology heterogeneity to assess external validity; and (4) include multiple models to map model‑dependent behavior. All follow‑ups should be preregistered with power plans aligned to expected baseline success rates.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired study with shared_initial_candidate semantics on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus, a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline produced a small absolute paired improvement (0.005) relative to a baseline single‑shot generator; the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test did not reach α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). Only five validator repairs were invoked and total model calls used = 1005. The primary inferential outcome is the preregistered exact McNemar result; a one‑sided McNemar reported here (p = 0.03125) was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration and is presented as exploratory/post‑hoc. These artifact‑grounded results indicate that downstream verifier/repair safeguards can prevent some unsafe outcomes, but measurable marginal gains are constrained when baseline outputs are already highly valid and when the paired design isolates downstream effects. We archive full preregistration, execution manifests, raw responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and encourage preregistered follow‑ups that broaden model diversity, validator coverage, and repair budgets.

limitations: Single‑model scope: only the declared model gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or versions.

Synthetic corpus and deterministic validator: tasks come from a synthetic stress corpus and validation used a deterministic digital twin (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); external validity to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments is limited.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired comparison isolates downstream validator/repair effects only; it does not measure differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompting arms that were not executed (those arms were not part of the frozen preregistration).

Low baseline failure prevalence: baseline success = 99.5%; the preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60 and a target effect of 0.15, so the observed baseline greatly reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains. This mismatch is reported explicitly and reduces the study's ability to detect very small practical effects using the preregistered confirmatory test.
Sparse repairs and interpretation limits: only five validator repairs were invoked, constraining inference about repair efficacy across failure modes.

Statistical nuance: the preregistered primary test is exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.001, 0.01] is a preregistered descriptive summary but is sensitive to sparse discordant counts; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) was computed post‑hoc and is explicitly labeled exploratory because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.

Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the emulator/validator's rule set; semantic and emergent multi‑device policy violations may be underrepresented in the validator's modeled constraints.
